research_concepts: unit-level heterogeneity (proportion with lift > 0, median lift > 2pp)
methodological_questions: How to define PNR failure objectively from play-by-play derived possessions?
What is the appropriate unit of analysis for testing a 'league-wide' counter claim?
How to measure lift for specifically pull-up jump shots following a PNR failure vs. other contexts?
What minimal per-unit sample size is necessary to test a median lift of 0.02 points per possession with adequate power?
How to control for game-situation confounders that could create spurious positive or negative lift?
How to avoid lookahead and selection biases when defining failure thresholds and subsequent efficiency?
evidence_establishes: No prior project studies of this specific question exist in the retrieval index; no historical evidence is available.
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether pull-up usage and efficiency genuinely change after PNR failure compared to other game contexts.
The typical effect size and variability of such a counter across teams or players.
The reliability of defining a PNR failure from possession-level points and contextual variables.
The statistical power achievable with the available data for the stated two-part threshold.
own_inferences: The research question is coherent but it defines a very demanding claim: at least 70% of units (e.g., team-seasons) must show a positive lift and the median lift must exceed 0.02 points per possession. Given typical per-unit sample sizes of 30–50 post-failure pull-up attempts per team-season, the standard error for the mean PPP is around 0.05–0.06; an effect of 0.02 is well below the detectable threshold per unit, so power to confirm the claim will be extremely low.

A definition of PNR failure based solely on a threshold (e.g., points ≤ median PNR PPP) is feasible with this data, but the choice of threshold is arbitrary and must be pre‑registered to avoid p‑hacking.

Confounders such as game score, time remaining and specific defensive matchups will affect both the tendency to run a pull‑up after a failure and the efficiency of that pull‑up; simple conditioning on the preceding possession’s outcome is unlikely to isolate a causal 'counter' effect.

The available data span four seasons, but the most recent season (2025‑26) is only partially available at the time of question; the test should be restricted to completed seasons to avoid lookahead, leaving three full seasons (2022‑23 through 2024‑25) for analysis, further reducing sample.
uncertainties: The exact distribution of possession types and pull‑up frequency after a PNR failure cannot be known without an exploratory analysis; the per‑unit sample size for post‑failure pull‑ups may be even smaller than the estimates used above, making the test infeasible.
The sport’s style may change over time; pooling across seasons assumes stationarity, which is uncertain.
Whether a ‘counter’ should be measured on the very next possession or over a longer window is unspecified; the choice has major consequences for sample size and interpretation.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical evidence was returned, so the decision is based entirely on an assessment of the data, the claim’s requirements and statistical power.

blocking_constraints.text: Per-unit sample size of post-PNR-failure pull-up jump shot possessions (likely 30–50 per team-season) is insufficient to detect a lift of 0.02 points per possession with reasonable power; usual effect sizes would be swamped by noise.
Defining an offensive PNR failure from play‑by‑play requires a pre‑registered threshold that may misclassify many true successes/failures, attenuating any true lift signal.

Post‑failure pull‑up efficiency is confounded by game context (score, time, quarter, defensive strength) that cannot be fully controlled without a causal design, inflating or masking the supposed counter effect.

prior_work.summary: No prior work on this precise claim was retrieved.

risks.text: The test requires precise within‑unit lift estimates; given the rarity of pull‑up attempts following a PNR failure and the small effect size stipulated (≥ 0.02 pp), optimistic power calculations show an unacceptably high risk of failing to detect even a real effect.

Play‑type classification (PNR vs. other) and shot‑type classification (pull‑up vs. other) rely on the accuracy of the derived possession data, which may contain errors; any misclassification will bias lift estimates toward zero.
Game situation (e.g., shot clock, score margin, opponent defensive alignment) is a strong confounder; failing to account for it could produce spurious lift or obscure a real counter.
Pull‑up jump shots are a minority of total possessions; conditioning on PNR failure further reduces the base rate, leading to low per‑unit sample sizes and volatile estimates.

design.estimand: Per‑unit (team‑season) difference in mean points per possession on possessions that end with a pull‑up jump shot, comparing those immediately following an offensive PNR failure (PNR possession scoring ≤ league‑wide median PNR points per possession, pre‑registered) vs. all other pull‑up possessions.
design.unit: Team‑season (30 teams × 3 full seasons, e.g. 2022‑23, 2023‑24, 2024‑25); units with fewer than 50 eligible post‑failure pull‑up attempts are excluded.
design.sample: All regular‑season possessions from the three complete seasons meeting the PNR and pull‑up criteria, stratified by team‑season.
design.power: Power analysis for the two‑part claim requires simulation. For a single team‑season with 40 post‑failure pull‑ups and a large comparison sample, the minimum detectable lift (80 % power, α = 0.05) is roughly 0.10–0.15 ppp, well above the required median of 0.02. To detect a median lift of 0.02 across units, either far more data per unit or a large number of units (e.g., many more seasons) would be needed, placing a conservative test out of reach with current data.
design.controls: Baseline pull‑up efficiency in that unit (overall, excluding post‑failure), game‑period fixed effects (quarter, minutes remaining), strength of opponent defense (rating), and binary indicators for back‑to‑back games to reduce confounding.
design.falsification: Falsification tests: (a) replace PNR failure with a random sampling of non‑PNR possessions of similar point outcome and test for lift, expecting no effect; (b) lag the counter window by two or three possessions and test for attenuation of lift.
design.multiplicity: The claim commits to a single shot type (pull‑up) and two summary statistics (proportion of positive‑lift units, median lift). No multiplicity adjustments are required if no other shot types or thresholds are tested; if alternative thresholds are explored, they would need to be specified as secondary.
design.decision_rule: Use a Bayesian hierarchical model with team‑season random effects on the lift parameter. Claim is supported if: (1) posterior probability that at least 70 % of units have true lift > 0 exceeds 0.95, and (2) posterior median of the median lift across units exceeds 0.02, with a 95 % credible interval not including negative values. A preregistered, one‑sided ‘super‑threshold’ test on the proportion and median would also be acceptable.
design.data_version: NBA 2022‑23, 2023‑24, 2024‑25 regular‑season play‑by‑play, substitution, matchup and derived play‑type possession data, frozen prior to analysis.

methodological_questions: How to define PNR failure reliably from play-by-play data?
What is the appropriate unit of analysis for testing a league-wide counter claim?
How to measure lift for a specific shot type as a counter to a defensive outcome?
What sample size per unit is required to test a threshold of median lift >2pp in at least 70% of units?
How to avoid selection bias and confounding when analyzing offensive counters to defensive failures?
args.query: If pick-and-roll fails defensively, is pull-up jump shot a real league-wide counter? Test requires lift >0 in >=70% of units with median lift >2pp.
